claim: The M4 muscarinic acetylcholine receptor (M4 mAChR) is a validated and clinically relevant allosteric drug target for several major psychiatric and cognitive disorders.
source: The M4 muscarinic acetylcholine receptor (M4 mAChR) is a validated and clinically relevant allosteric drug target for several major psychiatric and cognitive disorders.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge in the abstract without specific data in this manuscript, drawing on prior research in the field.

claim: LY2033298 (LY298) and VU0467154 (VU154) are positive allosteric modulators of the M4 mAChR.
source: In this study, we rigorously quantified the affinity, efficacy, and magnitude of modulation of two different positive allosteric modulators, LY2033298 (LY298) and VU0467154 (VU154), combined with the endogenous agonist acetylcholine (ACh) or the high-affinity agonist iperoxo (Ipx), at the human M4 mAChR.
evidence: The study directly characterizes these compounds as PAMs through experimental measurements.

claim: Cryo-EM structures of the M4 mAChR were determined bound to a cognate Gi1 protein and in complex with ACh, Ipx, LY298-Ipx, and VU154-Ipx.
source: By determining the cryo-electron microscopy structures of the M4 mAChR, bound to a cognate Gi1 protein and in complex with ACh, Ipx, LY298-Ipx, and VU154-Ipx, and applying molecular dynamics simulations, we determine key molecular mechanisms underlying allosteric pharmacology.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that these structures were determined in this study.

claim: Orthosteric and allosteric ligand–receptor–transducer complex stability plays a vital role in determining affinity, efficacy, cooperativity, probe dependence, and species variability.
source: In addition to delineating the contribution of spatially distinct binding sites on observed pharmacology, our findings also revealed a vital role for orthosteric and allosteric ligand–receptor–transducer complex stability, mediated by conformational dynamics between these sites, in the ultimate determination of affinity, efficacy, cooperativity, probe dependence, and species variability.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract, supported by the combined structural and dynamic studies.

claim: LY298 was the first reported highly selective PAM of the M4 mAChR and displayed antipsychotic efficacy in a preclinical animal model of schizophrenia.
source: Among these, LY2033298 (LY298) was the first reported highly selective PAM of the M4 mAChR and displayed antipsychotic efficacy in a preclinical animal model of schizophrenia (Chan et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: LY298 has been difficult to optimize with respect to its molecular allosteric parameters and shows variability of response between species.
source: Despite LY298 being one of the best characterized M4 mAChR PAMs, its therapeutic potential has been limited by numerous factors, including its chemical scaffold, which has been difficult to optimize with respect to its molecular allosteric parameters (Figure 1C) and variability of response between species (Suratman et al., 2011; Wood et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation, supported by citations.

claim: VU154 showed robust efficacy in preclinical rodent models but exhibited species selectivity that prevented its clinical translation.
source: In the search for better chemical scaffolds, the PAM, VU0467154 (VU154), was subsequently discovered. VU154 showed robust efficacy in preclinical rodent models; however, it also exhibited species selectivity that prevented its clinical translation (Bubser et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: LY298 and VU154 have very similar binding affinities for the allosteric site with pKB values of 5.65 ± 0.07 and 5.83 ± 0.12, respectively.
source: Analysis of these experiments revealed that LY298 and VU154 have very similar binding affinities for the allosteric site with values (expressed as negative logarithms; pKB) of 5.65 ± 0.07 and 5.83 ± 0.12, respectively (Table 1), in accordance with previous studies (Bubser et al., 2014; Leach et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result from radioligand binding assays.

claim: LY298 potentiated the binding affinity of ACh approximately 400-fold.
source: Both PAMs potentiated the binding affinity of ACh and Ipx (Figure 1E), with the effect being greatest between LY298 and ACh (~400-fold increase in binding affinity).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from binding experiments shown in Figure 1E.

claim: VU154 potentiated the binding affinity of ACh approximately 40-fold.
source: Comparatively, the positive cooperativity between VU154 and ACh was only 40-fold.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from binding experiments.

claim: LY298 potentiated the binding affinity of Ipx approximately 72-fold.
source: When Ipx was used as the agonist, the binding affinity modulation mediated by both PAMs was more modest, characterized by an approximately 72-fold potentiation for the combination of Ipx and LY298, and 10-fold potentiation for the combination of Ipx and VU154.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from binding experiments.

claim: VU154 potentiated the binding affinity of Ipx approximately 10-fold.
source: When Ipx was used as the agonist, the binding affinity modulation mediated by both PAMs was more modest, characterized by an approximately 72-fold potentiation for the combination of Ipx and LY298, and 10-fold potentiation for the combination of Ipx and VU154.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from binding experiments.

claim: The PAMs LY298 and VU154 display probe-dependent effects with respect to their ability to modulate the affinity of ACh versus Ipx.
source: These results indicate probe-dependent effects (Valant et al., 2012) with respect to the ability of either PAM to modulate the affinity of each agonist (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the differential modulation observed with different agonists, supported by citation.

claim: LY298 exhibits negative cooperativity with the antagonist [3H]-NMS.
source: A probe-dependent effect was also observed with the radioligand, [3H]-NMS, evidenced by a reduction in specific radioligand binding due to negative cooperativity between the antagonist probe and LY298, which has been previously reported (Chan et al., 2008; Leach et al., 2010; Suratman et al., 2011; Thal et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as an observed effect, supported by multiple citations.

claim: The rank order of efficacy in signaling assays was ACh > Ipx > LY298 > VU154.
source: Notably, in both signaling assays, the rank order of efficacy was ACh > Ipx > LY298 > VU154.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental results from TruPath and pERK1/2 assays.

claim: The rank order of transducer coupling was Ipx >> ACh ~ LY298 > VU154.
source: Consequently, in both assays, the rank order of transducer coupling was Ipx >> ACh ~ LY298 > VU154 due to Ipx having a higher binding affinity for the receptor.
evidence: This is a summary of calculated transducer coupling coefficients from experimental data.

claim: VU154 displayed lower positive functional cooperativity with ACh than LY298.
source: Notably, VU154 displayed lower positive functional cooperativity with ACh than LY298.
evidence: This is a direct comparison of functional cooperativity values from signaling assays.

claim: VU154 had negligible functional modulation with Ipx in the TruPath assay.
source: Strikingly, VU154 had negligible functional modulation with Ipx, in contrast to the cooperativity observed with ACh in the TruPath assay.
evidence: This is a direct observation from TruPath assay data.

claim: VU154 would be classified as a 'neutral' allosteric ligand with Ipx in the TruPath assay.
source: The tenfold difference in αβ values for VU154 between ACh and Ipx highlights the dependence of the orthosteric probe used in the assay (i.e. probe dependence); on this basis, VU154 would be classified as a 'neutral' allosteric ligand (not a PAM) with Ipx in the TruPath assay, that is, VU154 still binds to the allosteric site, but displays neutral cooperativity (αβ = 1) with Ipx (Table 1).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional cooperativity data.

claim: LY298 and VU154 appear to have a slight negative to neutral effect on agonist efficacy in the Gi1 TruPath and pERK1/2 assays.
source: Nevertheless, our analysis shows the PAMs LY298 and VU154 appear to have a slight negative to neutral effect on agonist efficacy in the Gi1 TruPath and pERK1/2 assays (Table 1), suggesting that the predominant allosteric effect exerted by these PAMs is mediated through modulation of binding affinity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the efficacy modulation (β) calculations.

claim: The structures of ACh-, Ipx-, LY298-Ipx-, and VU154-Ipx-bound M4R-Gi1 complexes were determined to resolutions of 2.8, 2.8, 2.4, and 2.5 Å, respectively.
source: The structures of ACh-, Ipx-, LY298-Ipx-, and VU154-Ipx-bound M4R-Gi1 complexes were determined to resolutions of 2.8, 2.8, 2.4, and 2.5 Å, respectively (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Table 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the cryo-EM structure resolutions achieved.

claim: The M4R-Gi1 complex structures are similar in architecture to other activated class A GPCRs, including the M1R-G11 and M2R-GoA complexes.
source: Overall, our M4R-Gi1 complex structures are similar in architecture to that of other activated class A GPCRs, including the M1R-G11 and M2R-GoA complexes (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a comparative structural analysis with reference to prior structures.

claim: Superposition of the M4R-Gi1 complexes revealed nearly identical structures with RMSD of 0.4–0.5 Å for the full complexes and 0.3–0.4 Å for the receptors alone.
source: Superposition of the M4R-Gi1 complexes revealed nearly identical structures with root mean square deviations (RMSD) of 0.4–0.5 Å for the full complexes and 0.3–0.4 Å for the receptors alone (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a quantitative structural comparison result.

claim: Ipx has greater than 1000-fold higher binding affinity than ACh.
source: Together, the smaller binding pocket of Ipx and more stable binding interactions with nearby residues that include W4136.48 likely explain why Ipx has greater than 1000-fold higher binding affinity than ACh.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison of binding affinities, supported by structural and simulation data.

claim: ACh undergoes higher fluctuations in the orthosteric site than Ipx in GaMD simulations.
source: GaMD simulations revealed that ACh undergoes higher fluctuations in the orthosteric site than Ipx (Figure 3E and F, Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a direct result from molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: The interactions of N1173.37, W1644.57, and W4136.48 with Ipx were more stable than those with ACh in GaMD simulations.
source: Similarly, the interactions of N1173.37, W1644.57, and W4136.48 with Ipx were more stable than those with ACh (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct result from molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: Both LY298 and VU154 bind directly above the orthosteric site in the extracellular vestibule (ECV).
source: Both LY298 and VU154 bind directly above the orthosteric site in the ECV that is composed of a floor delineated by the tyrosine lid, and 'walls' formed by residues from TM2, TM6, TM7, ECL2, and ECL3 (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the cryo-EM structures.

claim: VU154 underwent considerably higher fluctuations than LY298 with RMSDs ranging from 1.5 to 15 Å for VU154 and 0.8–2.1 Å for LY298 relative to the cryo-EM structures in GaMD simulations.
source: Notably, VU154 underwent considerably higher fluctuations than LY298 with RMSDs ranging from 1.5 to 15 Å for VU154 (Video 7) and 0.8–2.1 Å for LY298 (Video 8) relative to the cryo-EM structures (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: There are three key binding interactions shared between both PAMs and the M4 mAChR: a three-way π-stacking interaction between F18645.51, the aromatic core of the PAMs, and W4357.35; a hydrogen bond between Y4397.39 and the primary amine of the PAMs; and a hydrogen bond between Y892.61 and the carbonyl oxygen of the PAMs.
source: There are three key binding interactions that are shared between both PAMs and the M4 mAChR: (1) a three-way π-stacking interaction between F18645.51 (ECL2 residues have been numbered 45.X denoting their position between TM4 and TM5 with X.50 being a conserved cysteine residue), the aromatic core of the PAMs, and W4357.35; (2) a hydrogen bond between Y4397.39 of the tyrosine lid and the primary amine of the PAMs; and (3) a hydrogen bond between Y892.61 and the carbonyl oxygen of the PAMs (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the cryo-EM structures.

claim: During GaMD simulations, the key binding interactions were more stable with LY298 than VU154.
source: While these interactions are conserved for both PAMs in the consensus cryo-EM maps, during GaMD simulations these interactions were more stable with LY298 than VU154 (Figure 4H–K, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct result from molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: Mutation of Y892.61, F18645.51, W4357.35, or Y4397.39 to alanine completely abolished the binding affinity modulation mediated by LY298 and VU154 at the M4 mAChR.
source: The importance of these interactions was validated pharmacologically (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Table 4), whereby mutation of any of these residues completely abolished the binding affinity modulation mediated by LY298 and VU154 at the M4 mAChR with both Ipx and ACh as agonists.
evidence: This is a direct result from mutagenesis and binding experiments.

claim: The binding of LY298 is more stable than VU154 due to LY298 being able to form stable binding interactions with key residues in the ECV.
source: These results indicate that the binding of LY298 is more stable than VU154 due to LY298 being able to form stable binding interactions with key residues in the ECV. This provides a likely explanation for why LY298 was able to exert greater positive binding cooperativity on orthosteric agonists than VU154.
evidence: This is an interpretation combining structural, simulation, and pharmacological data.

claim: PAMs manifest higher cooperativity when interacting with agonists that are inherently less stable on their own when bound to the receptor, in contrast to more stable ligands.
source: These results provide a plausible mechanism for probe dependence, at least with regard to differences in the magnitude of the allosteric effect depending on the ligand bound. Namely, PAMs manifest higher cooperativity when interacting with agonists, such as ACh, that are inherently less stable on their own when bound to the receptor, in contrast to more stable ligands such as Ipx.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on GaMD simulation results comparing ACh and Ipx dynamics.

claim: In the presence of LY298 or VU154, the dynamics of ACh binding was decreased, with RMSFs reduced to 1.23 Å and 1.82 Å, respectively, and with LY298 having the greatest effect.
source: In the presence of LY298 or VU154, the dynamics of ACh binding was decreased, with RMSFs reduced to 1.23 Å and 1.82 Å, respectively, and with LY298 having the greatest effect (Figure 4—figure supplement 3F).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from GaMD simulations.

claim: LY298 is a stronger PAM-agonist than VU154 because it better stabilizes the active conformation of the M4 mAChR.
source: Overall, the GaMD simulations show that in the absence of agonist alone, or agonist and G protein, LY298 better stabilizes activation motifs from the top of the receptor (W4357.35) all the way down to the intracellular G protein binding pocket (DRY-TM6), providing mechanistic insights into the function of LY298 as a stronger PAM-agonist than VU154.
evidence: This is an interpretation of GaMD simulation results showing differential stabilization of active conformations.

claim: Mutation of W4136.48 to alanine significantly impaired the efficacy of ACh but only reduced the efficacy of LY298 by twofold.
source: Mutation of W4136.48 to alanine significantly impaired the efficacy of ACh but only reduced the efficacy of LY298 by twofold, such that ACh and LY298 had similar efficacy for this mutant (Figure 6G–I, Table 5).
evidence: This is a direct result from mutagenesis and functional assays.

claim: The functional modulation (αβ) between ACh and LY298 increased to over 3600 (a 20-fold increase vs. WT) at W413A6.48.
source: Interestingly, the functional modulation (αβ) between ACh and LY298 increased to over 3600 (a 20-fold increase vs. WT) at W413A6.48.
evidence: This is a direct result from mutagenesis and functional assays.

claim: The rotamer toggle switch residue W4136.48 is important for the signaling efficacy of orthosteric agonists and PAM-agonists but does not impair the process of functional allosteric modulation.
source: These results show that, at the M4 mAChR, the rotamer toggle switch residue is important for the signaling efficacy of orthosteric agonists and PAM-agonists but does not impair the process of functional allosteric modulation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the W413A mutagenesis results.

claim: W4136.48 has a strong role in maintaining the conformational dynamics of the receptor and is a key trigger for robust signal transduction.
source: Together with the observation that most of the structural differences between the active-state M4 mAChR structures occur at or above W4136.48, we propose that this residue has a strong role in maintaining the conformational dynamics of the receptor and is a key trigger for robust signal transduction.
evidence: This is a mechanistic proposal based on structural and mutagenesis data.

claim: At the mouse M4 mAChR, VU154 has a high degree of positive binding modulation, functional modulation, and allosteric agonism that is comparable to LY298 at the human M4 mAChR.
source: Conversely, at the mouse M4 mAChR, VU154 has a high degree of positive binding modulation, functional modulation, and allosteric agonism that is comparable to LY298 at the human M4 mAChR (Figure 7—figure supplements 1 and 2, Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct result from pharmacological experiments comparing human and mouse receptors.

claim: Only three residues differ between the human and mouse M4 mAChR in the transmembrane domain: V91 (L in mouse), D432 (E in mouse), and T433 (R in mouse).
source: As shown in Figure 7A, only three residues differ between the human and mouse M4 mAChR with respect to the transmembrane domain. Specifically, residue V91 (L in mouse) at the top of TM2 points into the lipid bilayer, and D432 and T433 (E and R in mouse), which are located at the top of TM7 and form part of the allosteric binding site near VU154.
evidence: This is a direct comparison of amino acid sequences.

claim: VU154 had a tenfold higher binding affinity for the Ipx-bound mouse M4 mAChR compared to the human receptor.
source: For LY298, there were no statistically significant differences in binding or function between species and across the mutants that were more than threefold in effect. In contrast, VU154 had a tenfold higher binding affinity for the Ipx-bound mouse M4 mAChR (compare Figure 1G with Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a direct result from binding experiments comparing human and mouse receptors.

claim: The affinity of VU154 increased by 2.5-fold at the D432E and T433R mutants and the triple mutant matched the affinity of the mouse receptor.
source: The affinity of VU154 increased by 2.5-fold at the D432E and T433R mutants and the triple mutant matched the affinity of the mouse receptor (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a direct result from mutagenesis and binding experiments.

claim: V91L, D432E, and T433R play a key role in mediating the species selectivity of VU154.
source: Nevertheless, these results indicate that V91L, D432E, and T433R play a key role in mediating the species selectivity of VU154.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mutagenesis results showing that these mutations affect VU154 activity.

claim: Both the D432E and T433R mutants resulted in a dynamic profile of VU154 that matched GaMD simulations of LY298 from the LY298-Ipx-bound M4R-Gi1 cryo-EM structure.
source: Excitingly, both the D432E and T433R mutants resulted in a dynamic profile of VU154 that matched our GaMD simulations of LY298 from the LY298-Ipx-bound M4R-Gi1 cryo-EM structure, including stabilized VU154 binding, constrained χ2 rotamer conformations of W4357.35 and W4136.48, and stable binding interactions with Y892.61, Y4397.39, Q18445.49, and F18645.51 (Figure 7D–K, Figure 7—figure supplement 3, Videos 9 and 10).
evidence: This is a direct result from GaMD simulations on mutant structures.

claim: Receptor dynamics play an important role in the determination of allosteric modulator selectivity.
source: Collectively, these findings reiterate the importance of receptor dynamics in the determination of allosteric modulator selectivity as even subtle differences in amino acid residues between species may result in profound changes in overall stability of the same PAM-agonist-receptor complex.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the species selectivity studies combining mutagenesis and simulations.

claim: ACh was a more efficacious agonist than Ipx despite having weaker interactions with the receptor.
source: The observation that ACh was a more efficacious agonist than Ipx (Table 1) yet bound with lower affinity and less stable interactions than Ipx was paradoxical.
evidence: This is a direct comparison of efficacy and binding data from pharmacological experiments.

claim: The ACh-bound M4 mAChR more readily sampled receptor conformations that engaged with the transducers.
source: One interpretation of these results was that the ACh-bound M4 mAChR more readily sampled receptor conformations that engaged with the transducers (Manglik et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the efficacy paradox, supported by citation.

claim: The ACh-bound M4 mAChR may have faster G protein turnover than Ipx due to Ipx-M4R-Gi1 forming a more stable ternary complex.
source: Similarly, the ACh-bound M4 mAChR may also have faster G protein turnover than Ipx due to Ipx-M4R-Gi1 forming a more stable ternary complex (Furness et al., 2016; Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a mechanistic speculation based on the stability differences observed, supported by citation.

claim: Two PAMs with distinctly different pharmacological profiles may bind to and stabilize receptor conformations that were very similar when viewed as static structures.
source: Indeed, if considering this issue from the perspective of allosteric modulators of GPCRs, our study highlights that two PAMs with distinctly different pharmacological profiles (Figure 1) may bind to and stabilize receptor conformations that were very similar when viewed as static structures (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a key observation from comparing the cryo-EM structures of LY298 and VU154 complexes.

claim: GaMD simulations of GPCRs bound to allosteric ligands could be an extremely valuable tool for drug discovery and optimization.
source: These observations were consistent with LY298 having greater positive binding cooperativity than VU154 (Figure 1E) and suggest that GaMD simulations of GPCRs bound to allosteric ligands could be an extremely valuable tool for drug discovery and optimization (Bhattarai and Miao, 2018).
evidence: This is a forward-looking statement about the utility of the simulation approach, supported by citation.

claim: Stabilizing the ECV region by PAMs likely leads to increased efficacy.
source: Prior work by DeVree et al., 2016 established that allosteric coupling of G proteins to the unliganded active receptor conformation promoted closure of the ECV region. This allosteric coupling is reciprocal and stabilizing the ECV region by PAMs likely leads to increased efficacy (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on prior work and the current findings, supported by citation.

claim: The degree of positive modulation for PAMs increases with an increase in the efficacy of the agonists according to the two-state receptor model.
source: Another explanation invokes the two-state receptor model (Canals et al., 2011), which stipulates that the degree of positive modulation for PAMs increases with an increase in the efficacy of the agonists. The pharmacology data support this model as ACh was more efficacious than Ipx and was better modulated by both PAMs (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the probe dependence data in the context of a theoretical model, supported by citation.

claim: Conformational dynamics between agonist and receptor are important for functional signaling.
source: These observations are also consistent with recent studies that suggest that conformational dynamics between agonist and receptor are important for functional signaling (Bumbak et al., 2020; Cary et al., 2022; Deganutti et al., 2022; O'Connor et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a general statement supported by multiple citations to recent literature.

claim: The M4R-Gi1 structures described in this study are of higher quality than those reported by Wang et al., 2022.
source: Unfortunately, the quality of density in the EM maps around the orthosteric and allosteric sites of these M4R-Gi1 structures (Wang et al., 2022) was poor, resulting in several key residues being mismodeled in each site (Figure 2—figure supplement 5). Therefore, differences between the M4R-Gi1 structures described herein and those by Wang et al., 2022 are highly likely to not be due to genuine differences and, as such, we compared the prior M1R-G11 and M2R-GoA complex structures (Maeda et al., 2019) in this study.
evidence: This is an implicit claim based on the comparison of map quality and modeling accuracy.

claim: The orthosteric site of the M4 mAChR is buried within the TM bundle in an aromatic cage composed of four tyrosine residues, two tryptophan residues, one phenylalanine residue, and seven other polar and nonpolar residues.
source: The orthosteric site of the M4 mAChR, in common with the other mAChR subtypes, is buried within the TM bundle in an aromatic cage that is composed of four tyrosine residues, two tryptophan residues, one phenylalanine residue, and seven other polar and nonpolar residues (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a direct structural observation from the cryo-EM structures.

claim: All 14 orthosteric binding site residues are absolutely conserved across all five mAChR subtypes.
source: Notably, all 14 of these residues are absolutely conserved across all five mAChR subtypes, underscoring the difficulty in developing highly subtype-selective orthosteric agonists (Burger et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about sequence conservation, supported by citation.

claim: Both ACh and Ipx have a positively charged trimethyl ammonium ion that makes cation-π interactions with Y1133.33, Y4166.51, Y4397.39, and Y4437.43.
source: Both ACh and Ipx have a positively charged trimethyl ammonium ion that makes cation-π interactions with Y1133.33, Y4166.51, Y4397.39, and Y4437.43 (Figure 3C; superscript refers to the Ballesteros and Weinstein scheme for conserved class A GPCR residues; Ballesteros and Weinstein, 1995).
evidence: This is a direct structural observation from the cryo-EM structures.

claim: Both ACh and Ipx have a polar oxygen atom that can form a hydrogen bond to the indole nitrogen of W1644.57.
source: Likewise, both ACh and Ipx have a polar oxygen atom that can form a hydrogen bond to the indole nitrogen of W1644.57 with the oxygen of Ipx also being in position to interact with the backbone of N1173.37 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a direct structural observation from the cryo-EM structures.

claim: The bulkier heterocyclic isoazoline group of Ipx makes a π-π interaction with W4136.48.
source: The largest chemical difference between ACh and Ipx is the bulkier heterocyclic isoazoline group of Ipx that makes a π-π interaction with the conserved residue W4136.48 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a direct structural observation from the cryo-EM structures.

claim: W4136.48 is part of the CWxP motif, also known as the rotamer toggle switch, a residue that typically undergoes a change in rotamer between the inactive and active states of class A GPCRs.
source: The residue W4136.48 is part of the CWxP motif, also known as the rotamer toggle switch, a residue that typically undergoes a change in rotamer between the inactive and active states of class A GPCRs (Shi et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a statement about a conserved structural motif, supported by citation.

claim: The size of the orthosteric binding pocket contracted from 115 Å3 when bound to tiotropium to 77 and 63 Å3 when bound to ACh and Ipx, respectively.
source: In contrast, mAChR agonists are typically smaller in size than antagonists and inverse agonists, and this is reflected in a contraction of the size of the orthosteric binding pocket from 115 Å3 when bound to tiotropium to 77 and 63 Å3 when bound to ACh and Ipx, respectively (Figure 3G and H; Tian et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a quantitative structural analysis result.

claim: In the ACh-bound structure, W4136.48 was in a conformation matching the inactive-state tiotropium-bound structure.
source: In the ACh-bound structure, W4136.48 was in a conformation matching the inactive-state tiotropium-bound structure (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is a direct structural comparison.

claim: W4136.48 sampled a larger conformational space in the ACh-bound structure than in the Ipx-bound structure in GaMD simulations.
source: GaMD simulations also showed that W4136.48 sampled a larger conformational space in the ACh-bound structure than in the Ipx-bound structure (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and G).
evidence: This is a direct result from molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: The predominate χ2 angle of W4136.48 was approximately 60° and 105° in the ACh-bound and Ipx-bound simulations, respectively.
source: The predominate χ2 angle of W4136.48 was approximately 60◦ and 105◦ in the ACh-bound and Ipx-bound simulations, respectively, corresponding to the cryo-EM conformations.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from GaMD simulations.

claim: The VU154-Ipx-bound complex had more dynamic movements in the allosteric pocket than the LY298-Ipx-bound complex in 3DVA analysis.
source: The LY298-Ipx-bound complex appeared similar to the Ipx-bound complex with LY298 being bound in the ECV (Video 5). In contrast, the 3DVA of the VU154 structure had more dynamic movements in the allosteric pocket that could reflect partial binding of VU154 (Video 6).
evidence: This is a direct observation from 3D variability analysis of cryo-EM data.

claim: Complexes bound to agonists with high affinity or co-bound with agonists and PAMs with high positive cooperativity exhibit lower dynamic fluctuations.
source: Therefore, the GaMD simulations corroborate our 3DVA results and suggest that complexes bound to agonists with high affinity or co-bound with agonists and PAMs with high positive cooperativity will exhibit lower dynamic fluctuations.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from comparing 3DVA and GaMD simulation results.

claim: Mutation of Q18445.49 to alanine had no effect on the binding affinity modulation of LY298 or VU154.
source: A potential fourth interaction was observed with residue Q18445.49 and the amide nitrogen of the PAMs; however, the GaMD simulations suggest that this interaction is relatively weak (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and H), consistent with the fact that mutation of Q18445.49 to alanine had no effect on the binding affinity modulation of LY298 or VU154 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Table 4).
evidence: This is a direct result from mutagenesis and binding experiments.

claim: Mutation of N4236.58 to alanine reduced the binding modulation of LY298.
source: For LY298, this is an interaction between the fluorine atom and N4236.58 that appeared to be stable during simulation and, when mutated to alanine reduced the binding modulation of LY298 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K, Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Table 4; Thal et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a direct result from mutagenesis and binding experiments, supported by citation.

claim: W4357.35 changes from a planar rotamer in the agonist-bound structures to a vertical rotamer that π stacks against the PAMs.
source: Finally, W4357.35 is a key residue in the ECV that changes from a planar rotamer in the agonist-bound structures to a vertical rotamer that π stacks against the PAMs (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is a direct structural observation comparing agonist-bound and PAM-agonist-bound structures.

claim: In GaMD simulations of the Ipx-bound structure, W4357.35 is predominantly in a planar conformation.
source: In GaMD simulations of the Ipx-bound structure, W4357.35 is predominantly in a planar conformation that corresponds to its conformation in the cryo-EM structure (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is a direct result from molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: The binding of LY298 stabilizes W4357.35 into a vertical position in GaMD simulations.
source: In contrast, the binding of LY298 stabilizes W4357.35 into a vertical position (Figure 4K).
evidence: This is a direct result from molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: In the VU154-bound receptor, W4357.35 appears to alternate between the planar and vertical positions in GaMD simulations.
source: However, in the VU154-bound receptor, W4357.35 appears to alternate between the planar and vertical positions, consistent with VU154 having a less stable binding pose (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is a direct result from molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: In the absence of PAM, ACh was more dynamic than Ipx with root-mean-square fluctuations (RMSF) of 2.13 Å versus 0.88 Å.
source: In the absence of PAM, ACh was more dynamic than Ipx with root-mean-square fluctuations (RMSF) of 2.13 Å versus 0.88 Å, reflective of the fact Ipx binds with higher affinity than ACh (Figure 4—figure supplement 3F).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from GaMD simulations.

claim: Agonist binding decreases the size of the orthosteric binding site primarily due to the tyrosine lid residue Y4166.51 undergoing a large rotation toward Y1133.33 creating a hydrogen bond.
source: As discussed previously, agonist binding decreases the size of the orthosteric binding site (Figure 3G and H). The primary driver of this decrease was the tyrosine lid residue Y4166.51, which underwent a large rotation toward Y1133.33 creating a hydrogen bond that seals off the tyrosine lid (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a direct structural observation from comparing inactive and active state structures.

claim: The closure of the tyrosine lid was further reinforced by a change in the rotamer of W4357.35 to a planar position that sits parallel to the tyrosine lid.
source: The closure of the tyrosine lid was further reinforced by a change in the rotamer of W4357.35 to a planar position that sits parallel to the tyrosine lid allowing for a π-π interaction with Y4166.51 and a positioning of the indole nitrogen of W4357.35 to potentially form a hydrogen bond with the hydroxyl of Y892.61 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a direct structural observation from the active state structures.

claim: The contraction of the orthosteric pocket led to a contraction of the ECV with a 5 Å inward movement of the top of TM6 and ECL3.
source: The contraction of the orthosteric pocket by the inward movement of Y4166.51 also led to a contraction of the ECV with a 5 Å inward movement of the top of TM6 and ECL3.
evidence: This is a quantitative structural observation.

claim: The top of TM5 was displaced outward by 4 Å forming a new interface between TM5 and TM6 stabilized by a hydrogen bond between T4246.59 and the backbone nitrogen of P1935.36 along with aromatic interactions between F1975.40 and F4256.60.
source: As a consequence, the top of TM5 was displaced outward by 4 Å forming a new interface between TM5 and TM6 that was stabilized by a hydrogen bond between T4246.59 and the backbone nitrogen of P1935.36 along with aromatic interactions between F1975.40 and F4256.60 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a quantitative structural observation.

claim: These TM5-TM6 interactions were specific to the active state structures and appear to be conserved as they were also present in the M1 and M2 mAChR active state structures.
source: These interactions were specific to the active state structures and appear to be conserved as they were also present in the M1 and M2 mAChR active state structures (Maeda et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a comparative structural observation supported by citation.

claim: The binding of LY298 and VU154 had a minimal impact on the conformation of most ECL residues.
source: The binding of LY298 and VU154 had a minimal impact on the conformation of most ECL residues, implying that the reorganization of residues in the ECV by orthosteric agonists contributes to the increased affinity of the PAMs (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is a structural observation with an interpretation about PAM affinity.

claim: The conformations of activation motifs were very similar across all four active-state M4 mAChR structures.
source: The conformations of these activation motifs were very similar across all four active-state M4 mAChR structures and were consistent with the position of these motifs across other active-state class A GPCR structures (Zhou et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a comparative structural observation supported by citation.

claim: Beyond the rotamer toggle switch residue W4136.48, there are no discernible differences between the agonist and PAM-agonist-bound structures in activation motifs.
source: In comparison to the ECV residues (Figure 5B), beyond the rotamer toggle switch residue W4136.48, there are no discernible differences between the agonist and PAM-agonist-bound structures, suggesting a shared activation mechanism for residues below W4136.48 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a comparative structural observation with mechanistic interpretation.

claim: In GaMD simulations, LY298 underwent lower RMSD fluctuations than VU154 before dissociating from the receptor in the absence of agonist.
source: In GaMD simulations, LY298 underwent lower RMSD fluctuations than VU154 before dissociating from the receptor (Figure 5D–G).
evidence: This is a direct result from molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: The conformations of W4357.35 and W4136.48 were better stabilized in the LY298-Ipx-bound systems in GaMD simulations.
source: Similarly, the conformations of W4357.35 and W4136.48 were better stabilized in the LY298-Ipx-bound systems, indicating that LY298 more strongly promotes an active receptor conformation (Figure 5H–K).
evidence: This is a direct result from molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: In the presence of the G protein, both PAMs stabilized an active conformation of the receptor based on the distances between TM3 and TM6.
source: In the presence of the G protein, both PAMs stabilized an active conformation of the receptor based on the distances between TM3 and TM6 (Figure 5P and Q).
evidence: This is a direct result from molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: Upon removal of the G protein, the VU154-bound M4 mAChR quickly transitioned toward the inactive conformation, while the LY298-bound M4 mAChR was more resistant to deactivation in GaMD simulations.
source: Upon removal of the G protein, the VU154-bound M4 mAChR quickly transitioned toward the inactive conformation, while the LY298-bound M4 mAChR was more resistant to deactivation in the GaMD simulations (Figure 5R and S).
evidence: This is a direct result from molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: Mutation of residues around the orthosteric and allosteric sites often resulted in a reduction in the binding affinity of either ACh or LY298 at their respective binding sites.
source: As expected, these studies revealed that mutation of residues around the orthosteric and allosteric sites often resulted in a reduction in the binding affinity of either ACh or LY298 at their respective binding sites, though the allosteric site was typically less affected (Figure 6A and B, Table 5).
evidence: This is a summary of mutagenesis results from prior studies.

claim: The binding affinity modulation between ACh and LY298 was largely affected by mutation of aromatic residues that link the orthosteric and allosteric sites.
source: In contrast, the binding affinity modulation between ACh and LY298 was largely affected by mutation of aromatic residues that link the orthosteric and allosteric sites (Figure 6C), implying a network of residues that were responsible for transmitting binding cooperativity between these two sites (Thal et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a summary of mutagenesis results with mechanistic interpretation, supported by citation.

claim: Residues that affect the efficacy of LY298 include nearly all of the residues that also affect ACh efficacy, along with residues that link to the allosteric site and surround the LY298 binding site.
source: Interestingly, residues that affect the efficacy of LY298 include nearly all of the residues that also affect ACh efficacy, along with residues that link to the allosteric site and surround the LY298 binding site (Figure 6E, Table 5).
evidence: This is a summary of mutagenesis results.

claim: The direct signaling of LY298 via the allosteric site is linked through a similar network of residues and requires a functional orthosteric site for the transduction of signaling.
source: This suggests that the direct signaling of LY298 via the allosteric site is nonetheless linked through a similar network of residues and requires a functional orthosteric site for the transduction of signaling, and that mechanism involves equivalent closure of the orthosteric binding site, consistent with the thermodynamic reciprocity of cooperativity (Canals et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of mutagenesis results, supported by citation.

claim: Residues Y892.61, N4326.58, W4357.35, and W4407.40, when mutated to alanine, significantly decreased the functional modulation between ACh and LY298.
source: Residues Y892.61, N4326.58, W4357.35, and W4407.40 were identified as residues that, when mutated to alanine, significantly decreased the functional modulation between ACh and LY298 (Figure 6F, Table 5).
evidence: This is a direct result from mutagenesis and functional assays.
